reason: Not functional: a news photograph in a story card. The picture conveys what it shows, the link's aria-label carries the headline, and the image's own alt describes the damaged highway accurately. Good informative alt, wrong corpus.
Same finding as fi-4890, fi-4891 and fi-4903: a video thumbnail inside a carousel tab labelled only by its position, "Slide 2".

Functional: a footer badge linking to the project's own site. The two sentences of text beside it already say the site is powered by Trac and invite the reader to visit, so the alt repeats what is already there.

Functional: an icon-only footer link to the project's Bluesky account. The alt names both whose account it is and which service, which is more than the glyph could convey and exactly what the destination is.
Functional: the logo links to the site's own root. The alt transcribes the wordmark and its tagline, which names the organisation rather than saying the link goes home.
Functional: a mega menu toggle. The button already displays "Why Coursera" and the chevron inside it is aria-hidden with no alternative text of its own.

Not functional: an infographic banner linking to the food safety pages. The graphic's job is to convey the four steps, and the alt describes them faithfully, which is the right thing to do for an informative image.

Functional: the logo links to the site root, and the link's own aria-label says so in as many words. The figure holding the SVG is aria-hidden, so this label is the only reference and it names the destination.
Functional: an icon-only footer link to the project's Twitter account. Same pattern as fi-10291 and a different destination: the alt names whose account and which service.

An avatar is a picture of the person the link leads to, so a content image rather than a functional graphic. The image carries no alt of its own, and the label on the link mixes the username with topic-list state.
Functional: a sponsor logo linking to that sponsor's site, where the company name is the destination. Same reasoning as fi-1723 and fi-1724.
Functional: a mega menu toggle. The button already displays "Solutions" and the aria-hidden chevron has no alternative text. Same template as fi-2372.
Functional: the navigation menu button. The label names the action, and the SVG title says the same thing, so the two descriptions agree instead of competing.
Functional: the header logo links to the agency's own root. The alt is the agency name, which a person on weather.gov already knows, rather than the fact that the link goes home.
Same finding as fi-10825: a generated letter avatar standing in for a person, used as a profile link. A content image, with no alt of its own.

Not functional: a book cover linking to the work. The cover conveys what the book looks like, and "Cover of: Eternauta" describes it accurately and briefly, which is the right call for an informative image.
Functional: a sponsor logo linking to that sponsor's site. The company name is the destination, even though the href is a campaign shortener.
Functional: the catalogue mega menu toggle, same template as fi-2296. The button displays "Explore", the label extends that text, and the chevron itself has no alternative text.
Functional: the masthead links to the site's own root. Both the link's aria-label and the image's alt are the bare publication name, so neither names the destination.

Functional: the search menu toggle, currently expanded. The label names the action in the direction it will actually go, "Hide search menu", and the markup carries both wordings so the label tracks the state. That is the state reporting the criteria ask for.
Same finding as fi-10825 and fi-10826: an avatar used as a link to the poster's profile, with no alt on the image itself.
Not functional: a book cover linking to the work. The alt also transcribes a three-line scholarly title in full, which is accurate and far past any length a person listening would tolerate.
Functional: a download button for the Linux packages. The button already reads "Linux", so the correct alt is empty, and "Linux Logo" both repeats it and names the picture.

Functional: the header logo links to the university's home page, and the alt is "UC Berkeley home". Brand plus destination, in three words. The footer logo on the same page, fi-2149, drops the last word and that is the whole difference.
Functional: the search submit button, so a form control rather than a toggle. The button displays its own text "Search", the SVG is aria-hidden, and no alternative text was written for the graphic.
Functional: closes the mobile menu. The button carries its own hidden text "Close Menu" and the sprite icon has no alternative text of its own.
Same finding as the other three Discourse avatars in this batch: a picture of the person the link leads to, with no alt on the image.
Not functional: a book cover on a reading list entry. The empty alt is correct, because the link's own text carries the list name, but a cover is a content image rather than a functional graphic.
Functional: a download button for the macOS packages. The button already reads "macOS", so "Apple Logo" repeats it in a different vocabulary and names the picture as well.
Functional: the footer logo links to the university's home page. The alt is the bare institution name. The header logo on the same page says "UC Berkeley home", which is what good looks like.
